How I Did It: Road Hopper

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

1981 again — funny how much of my golden era traces back to that one year. This was the game the parents actually liked, if you can believe that, because it looked like it was teaching their kid to look both ways before crossing a street. I had a regular, a mail carrier on his lunch break, who'd play exactly one frog's worth every day and then leave, win or lose. Never more than one credit. I used to set my watch by him.

What the remodel changed

The old one I built moved the frog with plain timers — a "moveCooldown" I just made up on the spot — and if you tapped a key while the frog was mid-hop, sometimes it just... didn't count. Robots fixed that with what they call "input buffering," which is a fancy way of saying the game remembers you pressed something even if it catches you between hops, and honors it the second you land. They also redid the river logic so you actually ride the log or turtle smoothly instead of teleporting a grid square at a time, and the turtles blink before they go under now — you get a fair warning, not a cheap drowning. Screen shakes when you get flattened. Feels a lot more fair than it has any right to.

The spell that did it

Build our Frogger game on the shared engine. Thirteen columns, traffic lanes, a river with logs and turtle groups that submerge — blink a warning before they go under. One hop per press, but buffer the input so a tap during a hop still fires the next one instantly. Five home bays at the top; landing in an empty one scores, filling all five levels you up. Put a fly in a bay sometimes for bonus points and a crocodile in one that should look dangerous before you hop in. A lady frog rides a log occasionally — carrying her home is worth extra. Thirty-second timer per frog, shown as a shrinking bar.

Under the hood

  • The frog's position is a real floating-point column, not just a grid index, so riding a log drifts you smoothly instead of snapping — the hop itself still locks to exactly one tile.
  • Every lane's cars and logs wrap around the screen edge instead of despawning, so the road never looks like it's "resetting."
  • Turtles cycle through three states on a timer — up, a blinking warning, then under — and the higher the level, the longer they stay under and the more often it happens.
  • Every hop, every vehicle, every log speed is multiplied by the frame's actual elapsed time, so it plays the same on a phone as it does on my shop's ancient laptop.
